## 38a.4 Theorems 28.4 and 28.5: The Two McGucken Laws of Nonlocality

The derivational content of [44] extends beyond the delayed-choice and quantum-eraser dissolution to two formal laws governing the origin and growth of quantum nonlocality itself. These laws are imported as Theorems 28.4 and 28.5 of the present paper; they constrain not merely the apparent retrocausation of delayed-choice and quantum-eraser experiments but the very establishment of nonlocal correlations in spacetime.

**Theorem 28.4 (First McGucken Law of Nonlocality, Grade 2; consolidates [44, §2.1, §8]).** *Two quantum systems A and B can be in an entangled state only if there exists a chain of local interactions A ↔ C₁ ↔ C₂ ↔ ⋯ ↔ Cₙ ↔ B such that each interaction in the chain is local (the interacting systems are at the same spacetime point or within each other's light cones) and each adjacent pair in the chain has shared a common local origin at some point in its causal past. Equivalently: only systems of particles with intersecting McGucken Spheres — with each McGucken Sphere centered on each respective particle's local origin event — can ever be entangled.*

**Proof.** The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic supplies the unique mechanism by which quantum coherence — the derivational prerequisite for entanglement — is established between systems. Coherence between systems A and B requires shared phase content of the four-dimensional wavefunction Ψ across A's and B's spatial supports. Phase content propagates along x₄ at +ic from every event; the locus of phase-correlated points reachable from any local event p is precisely the McGucken Sphere Σ₊(p) (Theorem 2.5). Therefore, systems A and B can share phase content — and hence support entanglement — only if their respective McGucken Spheres intersect, which occurs if and only if there exists a chain of local interactions through which their phase contents have been brought into correlation. No mechanism exists by which phase correlation can be established between systems whose McGucken Spheres do not intersect: such systems are causally disconnected, and the +ic monotonicity of x₄-advance forbids retrocausal phase establishment (Theorem 28.3). ∎

**Theorem 28.5 (Second McGucken Law of Nonlocality, Grade 2; consolidates [44, §2.2, §8]).** *The sphere of potential entanglement emanating from any local event p grows at the velocity of light c. At time t after event p, the McGucken Sphere Σ₊(p) has radius r = c(t - t_p); particles within this sphere may be entangled with the original event; particles outside cannot, because the expansion of x₄ has not yet reached them. The boundary of entanglement-possibility is exactly the light cone — the causal boundary of relativity — and the expansion of x₄ at c simultaneously generates the light cone of relativity, the expanding wavefront of Huygens' Principle, and the sphere of potential entanglement of quantum mechanics. All three are the same geometric object — the McGucken Sphere — viewed from different physical perspectives.*

**Proof.** The radius of the McGucken Sphere is r(t) = c(t - t_p) by definition (Theorem 2.5: the null hypersurface from p has r = c·Δt). The light cone of special relativity has the same equation (Theorem 6.4a, four-velocity budget). Huygens' wavefront from a point source has the same equation (Theorem of the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework establishing Huygens as content of dx₄/dt = ic: see [17]). All three are aspects of the single expansion of x₄ at +ic from p. The growth rate is uniquely c by the McGucken Principle. ∎

**Theorem 28.5a (Nonlocality IS the McGucken Sphere; Information Destruction as Sphere-Surface Dilution; Grade 2; consolidates Theorem 28.5 with [23] and the Second-Law content of §11).** *Quantum nonlocality is not merely enabled by the McGucken Sphere — it is the McGucken Sphere itself. The Sphere's spherically symmetric expansion at velocity c is the geometric mechanism by which information at a local source event p is dissipated, spread, and concealed in the probabilistic spread over the Sphere's expanding surface area A(t) = 4π c² (t − t_p)². The local probability density |ψ(x, t)|² integrated over A(t) is preserved (unitarity), but the local probability density at any single point on the Sphere decays as 1/A(t) = 1/[4π c² (t − t_p)²], producing the characteristic 1/r² intensity falloff of radiative fields, the 1/r² spread of detection probability in Born's rule, and the inverse-square-law content of all spherically-symmetric phenomena from Newtonian gravity through Coulomb to the holographic-screen content of [11] and [36]. The conjunction of (i) unitarity (information preserved on the Sphere's surface) and (ii) +ic-monotonic surface-area growth (information diluted over an unboundedly-growing surface) is the geometric content of quantum-mechanical information destruction: nothing is lost from the universe, but everything once-locally-coherent becomes ever-more-spread.*

**Proof.** The McGucken Sphere Σ₊(p) at coordinate time t has surface area A(t) = 4π R²(t) = 4π c² (t − t_p)² (Definition 4.1(a), Theorem 4 Part (a)). By the Born rule (Theorem 10.12), the probability density that a measurement performed at time t finds the quantum state at any specific point x on the Sphere is |ψ(x, t)|² with normalization ∫_Σ |ψ|² dA = 1 (unitarity, Theorem 10.0 + Theorem 4.4 of the Algebraic Channel; conservation of total probability under the McGucken-derived unitary evolution U(t) = exp(−i Ĥ t/ℏ)). For a spherically symmetric wavefunction ψ(r, t) at radius r = R(t) on the Sphere, |ψ(R(t), t)|² = 1 / A(t) = 1/[4π c² (t − t_p)²] by the normalization condition. As t increases, A(t) grows as (t − t_p)², so |ψ|² at any single point on the Sphere decays as 1/(t − t_p)². The total probability is preserved (unitarity), but the local probability per unit area on the Sphere is diluted by the +ic-monotonic surface-area growth. This is the geometric content of the Second Law's information destruction at the quantum level: information is preserved in the unitary sense (the Algebraic Channel), but its concentration at any local point decays as the Sphere's surface grows (the Geometric Channel). The two readings are joint forcings of dx₄/dt = ic at the Sphere's surface. ∎

**Corollary 28.5a.1 (Unification of unitarity and information destruction).** *Unitarity (information preserved) and information destruction (information spread over an expanding surface) are not contradictory but complementary — the Algebraic Channel and the Geometric Channel readings of the same dx₄/dt = ic at the Sphere. Unitarity is the algebraic-symmetry reading: the L² norm ∫_Σ |ψ|² dA is preserved under the unitary group U(t). Information destruction is the geometric-propagation reading: the integrand |ψ|² at any single point on the Sphere decays as 1/A(t). The resolution of the Black Hole Information Paradox (Theorem 31 of the present paper) — that information is preserved on the horizon's expanding surface in the holographic sense while being inaccessible from any local point inside or outside — is the same content applied to the cosmological-scale McGucken Sphere of the black-hole event horizon.*

**Corollary 28.5a.2 (Inverse-square laws as Sphere-surface dilution).** *Every inverse-square law in physics — Newton's law of gravitation F ∝ 1/r², Coulomb's law F ∝ 1/r², the radiative intensity I ∝ 1/r², the Born-rule probability density |ψ|² ∝ 1/r² for spherically symmetric emission — is the geometric consequence of dx₄/dt = ic distributing a conserved quantity over the Sphere's surface A(t) = 4π R²(t). The conserved quantity differs across sectors (energy flux for radiation, force-line density for inverse-square forces, probability for Born rule), but the 1/r² falloff is the same Sphere-surface dilution in every case. The McGucken Sphere is therefore the geometric origin of the inverse-square content of physics.*

**Remark (the geometric content of "spooky action at a distance").** Einstein's 1935 phrase *spukhafte Fernwirkung* — "spooky action at a distance" — characterized quantum nonlocality as physically unacceptable because it appeared to violate locality. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework dissolves this objection at the derivational level: the apparent "distant action" is the apparent distance between two points on a single McGucken Sphere expanded from a common source event. There is no action across separate localities; there is one expanding Sphere from one local origin event, and the two endpoints are correlated because they are connected through the Sphere's geometric structure. Einstein's locality intuition is preserved (no superluminal action between separate events); his nonlocality concern is preserved (the correlations are real and Bell-violating); and the apparent paradox dissolves because the two endpoints were never separate localities — they were two points on one Sphere from one local event, which is itself the McGucken-geometric extension of the very notion of "locality" beyond the point-locality of pre-1905 physics. *Locality* is x₄-locality at the Sphere surface; *nonlocality* is the apparent distance between two points on that surface; *information destruction* is the +ic-monotonic growth of that surface; *unitarity* is the conservation of the integrated probability on it. All four are aspects of dx₄/dt = ic.

**Relation to no-signaling.** The Second McGucken Law of Nonlocality is stronger than the no-signaling theorem. The no-signaling theorem states that *entanglement cannot be used to transmit information faster than c*; it constrains the use of existing entanglement. Theorem 28.5 states that entanglement cannot be established faster than c; it constrains the origin of entanglement itself. No-signaling is a consequence of Theorem 28.5 but does not imply it. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework supplies the derivational source: x₄ expands at exactly c from every event, so phase correlation reaches no point faster than c.

## 38a.5 Theorem 28.6: The New York–Los Angeles Falsifiability Theorem

**Theorem 28.6 (New York–Los Angeles Falsifiability of the McGucken Nonlocality Principle, Grade 2; consolidates [44, §3]).** *Let electron A be located in a laboratory in New York and electron B be located in a laboratory in Los Angeles, with both electrons' positions, spins, and momenta continuously measured and found to exhibit no correlation. The McGucken Nonlocality Principle (Theorems 28.4 and 28.5) makes the falsifiable prediction: it is impossible to entangle electrons A and B without some form of local contact, either directly or through a locally-originated intermediary. To falsify the McGucken Nonlocality Principle, one would need to demonstrate a method for entangling A and B satisfying all of the following: (i) the electrons are never brought into direct local contact; (ii) no intermediary particle or system that has shared a local origin with either electron is used to mediate the entanglement; (iii) the entanglement is established faster than the velocity of light. No such method has been demonstrated or proposed in any interpretation of quantum mechanics, in any extension of the Standard Model, or in any thought experiment consistent with the known laws of physics.*

**Proof.** Every known method for entangling distant particles requires a locally-originated intermediary. The standard procedure — entanglement swapping (Żukowski et al. 1993) — operates as follows: (a) prepare two entangled pairs, particles C and D entangled at event E₁, and particles E and F entangled at event E₂; (b) transport C to New York and let it interact locally with electron A; transport F to Los Angeles and let it interact locally with electron B; (c) perform a Bell-state measurement on particles D and E at some intermediate location. After the Bell-state measurement, electrons A and B become entangled, but only because the chain A ↔ C (local in New York) ↔ D (shared McGucken Sphere from E₁) ↔ E (intersecting McGucken Spheres at Bell measurement) ↔ F (shared McGucken Sphere from E₂) ↔ B (local in Los Angeles) connects them through a sequence of locally-originated contacts. Every link in this chain is either a shared McGucken Sphere (from a common local creation event) or an intersection of McGucken Spheres (at a local measurement event). The final A–B entanglement traces back, through this chain, to the local creation events E₁ and E₂. All nonlocality begins in locality. Quantum teleportation (Bennett et al. 1993) has the same structure: entanglement is transferred, not created from nothing, at local intersections of McGucken Spheres.

The principle is therefore falsifiable in the strict Popperian sense: a single experimental or thought-experimental demonstration of entanglement established without a chain of local contacts would refute Theorems 28.4 and 28.5. To date, no such demonstration exists. ∎

**Significance.** Theorem 28.6 supplies the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework with explicit empirical content at the foundational level: the framework forbids a specific operationally testable phenomenon (the establishment of long-range entanglement without local origin), and the persistent failure of any proposed mechanism to achieve this falsifying outcome constitutes ongoing empirical confirmation. The framework does not merely accommodate the observed structure of quantum nonlocality (as standard interpretations do); it predicts the structure by deriving it from dx₄/dt = ic.

## 38a.6 Theorem 28.7: Six Independent Geometric Proofs of Expanding-Wavefront Nonlocality

The derivational foundation of the McGucken Nonlocality Principle rests on a specific geometric claim — that the expanding wavefront generated by dx₄/dt = ic is a genuine nonlocal entity whose spatially separated points share a common identity traceable to a local origin. The claim is established rigorously by six independent mathematical arguments, each framing the same physical object in the language of a different discipline.

**Theorem 28.7 (Six-Framework Geometric Nonlocality of the McGucken Sphere, Grade 2; consolidates [44, §4]).** *The expanding McGucken Sphere Σ₊(p) is a geometric locality in six independent mathematical senses, each of which establishes that its spatially separated points share a common identity traceable to a single local origin event p:*

*(i) **Foliation theory**: Σ₊(p) defines a foliation of three-dimensional space by nested 2-spheres S²(t) parameterized by time, with each sphere a leaf of the foliation carrying well-defined transverse geometry; all points on a leaf share common identity as members of the same leaf.*

*(ii) **Level sets of a distance function**: Σ₊(p) is the level set d(x) = c(t - t_p) of the distance function from p; every point on the wavefront is equidistant from p in the induced metric, sharing a common metric identity.*

*(iii) **Caustics and wavefronts (Huygens)**: Σ₊(p) is the envelope of secondary Huygens wavelets emanating from every point on the previous wavefront; all points on Σ₊(p) have the same causal status as the boundary of the causal future of p.*

*(iv) **Contact geometry**: in the jet space with coordinates (x₁, x₂, x₃, t), the growing wavefront traces a cone that is a Legendrian submanifold of the contact structure; all points on the Legendrian submanifold share a common contact-geometric identity.*

*(v) **Conformal and inversive geometry**: growing spheres under inversion map to other spheres or to planes; the family of expanding wavefronts belongs to a pencil in the inversive/Möbius geometry of space, sharing a common conformal identity invariant under the conformal group.*

*(vi) **Null-hypersurface locality (the deepest sense)**: under the Lorentzian line element ds² = dx² + dy² + dz² − c²dt², the growing wavefront is precisely a null-hypersurface cross-section — the intersection of the light cone with a spacelike slice — which is the canonical geometric locality in Minkowski geometry, being neither spacelike nor timelike but causally extremal, with every point on the wavefront having the same null-hypersurface identity relative to the source p.*

**Proof.** Each of the six framings is a standard construction in its respective mathematical discipline. The foliation by S²(t) follows from the smooth dependence of the McGucken Sphere on the parameter t. The level-set characterization is immediate from r(t) = c(t - t_p). The Huygens envelope is the wavefront-construction theorem of geometrical optics. The Legendrian submanifold structure follows from the contact-geometric formulation of wave propagation (Arnold *Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics*). The inversive-geometric structure follows from the action of the conformal group on the space of spheres. The null-hypersurface identification follows directly from ds² = 0 along the wavefront under the Minkowski metric. Each framing establishes the same conclusion — that the wavefront's spatially separated points share a common geometric identity traceable to a single local origin — in its own language. ∎

**Significance.** The six framings are mutually reinforcing: each frames the same physical object (the expanding wavefront) in the language of a different mathematical discipline, and each yields the same conclusion. This derivational multi-framing is itself evidence that the McGucken Sphere is the foundational geometric atom of nonlocality: an entity recognized as a single coherent object across six independent mathematical traditions. What appears from a three-dimensional perspective as a collection of causally disconnected points is, in the full four-dimensional geometry, a single unified object.

**Corollary 28.9 (Nonlocality Arrow as Derived Sixth Arrow, Grade 2; consolidates [44, §8 Corollary]).** *The growth of nonlocality established by the Second McGucken Law (Theorem 28.5) constitutes a derived sixth arrow of time, joining the five conventional arrows of Theorem 5 (thermodynamic, cosmological, radiative, psychological/biological, quantum-measurement) as manifestations of the one-way +ic expansion of the fourth dimension. All six arrows are projections of one underlying arrow — the +ic-monotonic advance of x₄ at every event. The title's "five arrows" framing is preserved as the canonical count; the sixth (nonlocality) arrow is a derivational consequence further unifying the framework with quantum nonlocality.

## 38a.9 Theorem 28.10: The Entangled-Pair Correlation as Two First-Contact Collisions of One Emitter Sphere

**McGucken Principle anchor.** Under dx₄/dt = ic, an entangled pair produced at source event p_E propagates as two photons on null worldlines of the single McGucken Sphere Σ₊(p_E). Each photon's detection is a first-contact collision (Theorem 10.13 of §14.10) between Σ₊(p_E) and the corresponding detector's absorber Sphere. The two detections are two collision events sharing one common Sphere — Σ₊(p_E) — and the correlations Bell 1964 formalized descend from that shared origin, not from any signal exchanged between the two detection events.

**Theorem 28.10 (Entangled-Pair Correlation as Two First-Contact Collisions, Grade 2; consolidates Theorem 10.13 of §14.10 above, Theorem 28.4 (First McGucken Law of Nonlocality) of §38a.1, and Theorem 28.5 (Second McGucken Law of Nonlocality) of §38a.2).** *Let a photon pair be produced by spontaneous parametric down-conversion (or any other coherent pair-production process) at event p_E. Let Σ₊(p_E) denote the emitter's McGucken Sphere. Let {p_A^(k)}_A and {p_B^(m)}_B denote the ensembles of candidate absorber events at detector A and detector B respectively. On any single pair-detection trial, the joint detection event at A is a first-contact collision of Σ₊(p_E) with one absorber Sphere Σ₊(p_A^(k*)) on the A-side, and the joint detection event at B is a first-contact collision of Σ₊(p_E) with one absorber Sphere Σ₊(p_B^(m*)) on the B-side. The geometry supplies the definiteness of each side (one pointlike collision, one absorber realized per side per trial) and, through the SO(3)-invariant Sphere measure, the joint Born distribution over (k*, m*) across many trials; the per-trial specific identities of k* and m* are the determinism-vs-chance seed the framework leaves open, at the fork every framework reaches. The correlated joint statistics arise because both collision events trace to one common Sphere Σ₊(p_E), not from any signal exchanged between the two detection events.*

**Proof.** By Theorem 10.13 of §14.10, each measurement event is a first-contact collision between an emitter Sphere and an absorber Sphere. For the entangled pair, both photons carry the same Σ₊(p_E) (the single Sphere from the shared source event). Detector A's registration event is a first-contact collision of Σ₊(p_E) with one A-side absorber Sphere Σ₊(p_A^(k*)); detector B's registration event is a first-contact collision of Σ₊(p_E) with one B-side absorber Sphere Σ₊(p_B^(m*)). The joint distribution over outcomes is bilinear in the two Sphere-collision amplitudes summed over the shared Σ₊(p_E) phase content, giving the entangled two-particle Born rule ρ_AB = |⟨ψ_A ⊗ ψ_B|Ψ_ent⟩|² for the entangled state Ψ_ent. Because both collision events involve the same Sphere Σ₊(p_E), the phase content at A and the phase content at B are correlated by their shared Sphere origin. This is the collision-level reading of the shared-Sphere content of Theorem 28.4 (First McGucken Law of Nonlocality). ∎

**No signal is exchanged.** Each detection event is its own pointlike first-contact collision of two Spheres; the two collisions are independent events on the McGucken manifold. The correlations descend from the fact that both collisions involve the same emitter Sphere Σ₊(p_E), not from any communication between the two detection events. The +ic monotonicity of the Sphere expansion forbids the reverse geometry (a Sphere contracting from one detection event to influence the other), so no retrocausal influence is possible either. The Bell correlations are read off the shared Sphere; the no-signaling constraint is preserved automatically because no Sphere-collision event transmits information to the other Sphere-collision event.

## 38a.10 Theorem 28.11: The Al-Khalili / Maudlin Signaling Seam Decided — Nonlocality Cloaked in Probability, Both Faces of One Sphere

**McGucken Principle anchor.** Under dx₄/dt = ic, genuine instantaneous nonlocality (the shared Sphere carrying phase-correlations across separated detection events) and no-signaling (the SO(3)-invariant Sphere measure flattening the marginal at each detector) are joint consequences of the same expansion, not two commitments to be reconciled. It's quantum connectivity is non-local. It's, it's instantaneous. What happens here affects what happens over there. The fact that I can't use it to send signals faster than light, tough luck on me. But maybe one day we'll find a way of doing it. Who knows?"* Curt Jaimungal reports to Al-Khalili at 1:22:53 that Tim Maudlin holds the stronger position that with genuine nonlocality plus the block universe, *"you could signal... theoretically you can."* Al-Khalili accepts the dilemma unresolved: *"if relativity then has to fall, then the block universe itself is no longer a valid picture. It's a big price to pay, but it can't be ruled out."*

**Theorem 28.11 (The McGucken No-Signaling Theorem Decides the Al-Khalili / Maudlin Seam, Grade 2; consolidates Theorem 28.5 of §38a.2 (Second McGucken Law of Nonlocality; the "stronger than no-signaling" clause), Theorem 10.13 of §14.10 (first-contact collision), Theorem 28.5a of §38a.4 (Sphere-surface dilution), and Theorem 28.10 of §38a.9 (entangled-pair as two first-contact collisions of one emitter Sphere)).** *Under dx₄/dt = ic, the same SO(3)-invariant McGucken-Sphere expansion at rate c that supplies the genuine instantaneous nonlocality (the shared Sphere Σ₊(p_E) carrying phase-correlations across separated detection events) also supplies the Born-rule marginal at each detector that flattens the outcome distribution, so the channel exists geometrically and transmits no information. Neither Al-Khalili's "maybe one day we can signal" nor Maudlin's "you could signal, theoretically you can" survives the derivation. The instantaneous influence is real (against Al-Khalili's "quantum correlations"-only reading), and no manipulation of the entanglement can transmit a signal (against Maudlin's "you could signal"). Both features are joint consequences of one Sphere geometry, not two commitments to be reconciled.*

**Proof.** Six steps.

*Step 1 (The instantaneous influence is real).* By Theorem 28.4 (First McGucken Law of Nonlocality, §38a.1), entanglement requires the two systems to share intersecting McGucken Spheres traceable to a common local origin. By Theorem 28.10 of §38a.9, an entangled pair produced at source event p_E carries the single Sphere Σ₊(p_E) to both detection sites; the two detection events are two first-contact collisions of that single Sphere with two absorber Spheres. The correlations between the two detection events are read from the shared Σ₊(p_E), which is one physical object visited at two spacetime events. The "instantaneous influence" content that Al-Khalili's genuine-nonlocality position asserts is real in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework: the two detection events are correlated by their shared Sphere origin, and the correlation is not a mere correlation of pre-existing hidden variables — it is a geometric identity on one expanding physical object. Al-Khalili's insistence that "quantum connectivity is non-local" is correct, and the framework supplies its physical mechanism.

*Step 2 (The marginal at each detector is SO(3)-symmetric).* By Theorem 7 of [12] and the SO(3)-invariant Sphere structure of Definition 4.1 property (b), the McGucken Sphere carries a unique SO(3)-invariant measure — the Haar measure on the sphere's rotation group. The Born rule content of the Sphere (Theorem 28.5a of §38a.4) supplies the probability density |ψ|² ∝ 1/A(t) on the Sphere's surface, which is SO(3)-symmetric in the direction sector. When the detector at either site A or B measures a specific observable direction (a specific spin projection, a specific polarization axis), the marginal outcome distribution at that detector is the projection of this SO(3)-invariant measure onto the chosen observable direction. The SO(3)-invariance forces the marginal to be flat in the observable direction: at each detector, viewed marginally (without conditioning on the outcome at the other detector), the outcome distribution is uniform over the observable's eigenvalue spectrum. This is the no-signaling content: no manipulation of the entangled state at one detector changes the marginal outcome distribution at the other detector.

*Step 3 (One measure produces both content).* The measure that produces the correlations in Step 1 and the measure that flattens the marginals in Step 2 are the same measure: the SO(3)-invariant Haar measure on Σ₊(p_E)'s surface. The correlations are read from the joint distribution over the two detection events' outcomes; the marginals are read from that same joint distribution projected onto each detector alone. The correlations exist because the joint distribution is non-factorizable (the two outcomes share the phase content of one Sphere); the marginals flatten because the SO(3)-symmetric measure has no preferred direction in the observable sector. Non-factorizability of the joint distribution and SO(3)-symmetry of the marginal are two properties of one measure on one Sphere — they are derivationally inseparable in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework.

*Step 4 (Al-Khalili's "maybe one day" is decided against).* Al-Khalili's "tough luck we can't use it to signal... but maybe one day we'll find a way" position leaves open the possibility that the no-signaling constraint might be overcome by some future clever protocol. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework decides this against Al-Khalili: no future protocol can overcome the no-signaling constraint, because the SO(3)-symmetry of the marginal at each detector is the derivational fact that the same measure produces both the correlations and the marginals — an operational hurdle it is not, and the reason is derivational. Any protocol that could manipulate the marginal at one detector to encode a signal would have to break the SO(3)-symmetry of the Sphere measure — which would also destroy the correlations that make the entanglement genuine in the first place. The instantaneous influence exists forever; the signaling capability is forever absent; both facts descend from the same Sphere expansion.

*Step 5 (Maudlin's "you could signal, theoretically you can" is decided against).* Maudlin's stronger position that genuine nonlocality plus the block universe should allow signaling rests on the premise that "genuine" nonlocality means transmittable influence. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework decides this against Maudlin: the nonlocality is genuine (one shared Sphere, real physical object, real instantaneous phase-correlation) and it is nevertheless untransmittable, because the same Sphere geometry that makes the correlation real is what flattens the marginals. Maudlin's inference that genuine nonlocality entails signaling capability confuses the correlation content (which is real and instantaneous) with the marginal-manipulation content (which is forbidden by the SO(3)-symmetry of the measure). The two are separable properties of the joint distribution: correlations live in the joint, no-signaling lives in the marginal, and both descend from one Sphere.

*Step 6 (Relativity is preserved without discarding genuine nonlocality — Cloaking Theorem 39).* Al-Khalili's dilemma at 1:23:00 — "if relativity then has to fall, then the block universe itself is no longer a valid picture. It's a big price to pay, but it can't be ruled out" — is a false dichotomy under the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework. Relativity's no-signaling constraint is preserved because the marginal is flat at each detector, so no signal is transmitted between spacelike-separated events. Genuine nonlocality is preserved because the correlations are non-factorizable, real, and read from one shared Sphere. The Cloaking Theorem 39 of the corpus [24; imported at Theorem 41 of §51.6 (McGucken Invariance) of the present paper and stated at [238, §V.6.4] in the measurement paper] supplies the mechanism that closes the dilemma completely: the preferred x₄-foliation to which the shared-Sphere coincidence is referred (the CMB rest frame of Theorem 40 of §51) is locally undetectable — its bookkeeping quantities cancel from every local invariant measurement any observer performs — so the nonlocality carries no signal (Steps 2–3 above) and produces no operational conflict with local Lorentz invariance. The framework is nonlocal in Brukner's 2018 classification of no-go dispositions (see §68b.13a below), retaining assumptions (1)(3)(4) and relinquishing (2) with the physical mechanism supplied by x₄-coincidence, not with a bare posit. The active growing block (Theorem 36 of §48) replaces the static block that Maudlin's argument requires, so the retrocausation branch of Al-Khalili's dilemma does not arise (see also Theorem 28.3 of §38a.3 for the no-retrocausation content). Al-Khalili's "big price to pay" is not the price the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework charges; the framework retains local Lorentz invariance, genuine nonlocality, the active growing block, and the +ic-monotonic directionality of time all together, as joint consequences of one principle, with the Cloaking Theorem 39 supplying the mechanism that keeps the preferred foliation locally invisible. ∎

**Consequence: Shimony's "peaceful coexistence" as one derivation, not two commitments.** Abner Shimony 1978 named the mysterious calibration between quantum mechanics' nonlocality and relativity's no-signaling constraint "peaceful coexistence," and characterized the mystery as the following: QM's nonlocality is real, relativity's no-signaling is real, and it is a remarkable and unexplained fact that the two coexist. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework explains the coexistence: the two features are not independently postulated and then found miraculously compatible; they are joint consequences of one geometric fact — the SO(3)-invariant expansion of the McGucken Sphere at +ic from each source event. What Shimony called "peaceful coexistence" is Theorem 28.11: nonlocality is the wavefront's identity (one Sphere connecting the two detection events); no-signaling is the wavefront's intensity (SO(3)-flat marginals from the Sphere's Haar measure); they are two faces of one Sphere. The calibration Shimony flagged as mysterious is forced, both features being projections of one object.

**The two-position seam and its resolution.** The Al-Khalili / Maudlin dispute — Al-Khalili's "we cannot signal but maybe one day we will" versus Maudlin's "we should be able to signal, given genuine nonlocality plus block universe" — is the sharpest live dispute in the contemporary literature on quantum nonlocality and relativity. Both positions rest on treating nonlocality and no-signaling as independently postulable features that might or might not coexist. Theorem 28.11 replaces the independent-postulation reading with a joint-derivation reading: one Sphere generates both the correlations and the marginal-flattening; no protocol can separate them; no manipulation of one detector's marginal can transmit information because the marginal-flattening is the same measure that makes the correlation. The seam is decided: never, in either direction. Al-Khalili's "maybe one day" is closed; Maudlin's "you could signal" is closed; both from opposite premises on one derivation.

**Comparison with standard treatments of no-signaling.** The Eberhard 1978 and Ghirardi–Rimini–Weber 1980 no-signaling theorems establish that entanglement cannot be used to transmit information faster than c — they constrain the *use* of existing entanglement. Theorem 28.5 of §38a.2 states the stronger content that entanglement cannot be *established* faster than c — it constrains the *origin* of entanglement. Theorem 28.11 of the present subsection states the additional content that the *same* SO(3)-symmetry that carries the correlations flattens the marginals — supplying the derivational reason for the no-signaling constraint, not just the constraint itself. The three theorems form a chain: origin (Theorem 28.5) → geometry (one shared Sphere, Theorem 28.10) → derivational unification of correlation and no-signaling (Theorem 28.11). The chain replaces three independent postulates (existence of entanglement, no-signaling of correlations, calibration between them) with three derived consequences of one principle dx₄/dt = ic.



# PART VI — TIME IN COSMOLOGY

# 38b. The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic Reading of Single-Photon Detection: The Opacity of One Photon and the Ensemble Recovery of Distance

The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality. A photon emitted at an event $p_E$ rides the McGucken Sphere of $p_E$: the fixed-$t$ cross-section $M^+_{p_E}(t)$, a 2-sphere of spatial radius $\rho = c(t - t_E)$, carries the photon's Born probability as the SO(3)-Haar measure on its surface (Theorem 10.1, §14.2). This section establishes a two-reading result about that one physical object. A single detection reads one event of the Sphere and returns neither the photon's travel distance nor its emission time, conserving the photon's phase and its emission present along a null worldline (Theorem 28.2, §38a.2); an ensemble of detections reads the Sphere's probability measure as a number flux falling with the inverse square of distance, and recovers the distance that one photon could not. The single-photon reading and the ensemble reading are the same expanding McGucken Sphere, and the Sphere's nonlocal probability is carried in both while being exhibited only in the second.

## 38b.1 The Single Photon Conserves Its Present and Hides the Sphere

The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality. Under the Principle a photon's worldline is null: its share of the expansion is $v_{x_4} = 0$ (absolute rest in $x_4$, mode 2 of Theorem 3), while the rate $dx_4/dt = ic$ holds at every event the photon crosses. The photon therefore accumulates no $x_4$-advance along its own worldline, and its proper time and proper length between emission and detection are zero (Theorem 28.2, §38a.2). The phase it carries — its unitary evolution — and the present of its emission event reach the detector unchanged.

A single detection registers one spacetime event $(t_\text{det}, \mathbf{x}_\text{det})$. The emission event $p_E = (\tau_0, \mathbf{x}_E)$ lies on the past McGucken Sphere through $\mathbf{x}_\text{det}$: the source distance $r = |\mathbf{x}_\text{det} - \mathbf{x}_E|$ and the emission time $\tau_0$ enter the detection only through the null relation $r = c(t_\text{det} - \tau_0)$. With $\tau_0$ unknown, one detection fixes neither $r$ nor $\tau_0$ separately. This is Theorem 10.8 (M1′, §14.8): no measurement protocol localizes the source to a point; the minimal localization is a 2-sphere of radius $c(t_\text{det} - \tau_0)$ parameterized by the unknown emission time, with source-position entropy bounded below by $S_\text{loc} = k_B \ln(4\pi r^2)$.

*Prior art (Einstein, Fifth Solvay Conference, 1927).* Einstein raised the single-particle expanding wave in the general discussion of the 1927 Solvay Conference. A particle emitted from a point produces a wavefunction that spreads as a spherical wave, and a detection localizes it to one point of the sphere. Einstein objected that reading $|\psi|^2$ as the probability of finding the particle at a given point of the sphere "assumes an entirely peculiar mechanism of action at a distance" (Einstein, 1927 Solvay general discussion, as presented in [250]; standard reproduction and translation in Bacciagaluppi and Valentini [249]). Einstein took the single-detection localization of the expanding spherical wave to be a difficulty for the theory.

*McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic reading.* The expanding spherical wave of Einstein's objection is the McGucken Sphere $M^+_{p_E}(t)$ of the emission event, the physical cross-section of $x_4$'s advance at $+ic$ (Definition 4.1; Theorem 10.1). The single detection reads one event of that Sphere and returns only the null constraint $r = c(t_\text{det} - \tau_0)$ (Theorem 10.8), with the photon's phase and emission present conserved along the null worldline (Theorem 28.2). The localization to one point is the quantized reading of the Sphere at one event; the Sphere's SO(3)-distributed probability over the full surface $4\pi r^2$ is carried by the photon but is not exhibited by the single outcome. The difficulty Einstein recorded is, under the Principle, the single-photon opacity of the Sphere: one detection conserves the photon's unitarity and present and holds the Sphere's nonlocal probability without displaying it.

## 38b.2 The Ensemble Reveals the Sphere as the Inverse-Square Flux

The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality. The same SO(3)-Haar Born measure that is opaque in one photon (§38b.1) is the measure of the whole Sphere surface, and over many photons it is read as a number flux. The Born density on the fixed-$t$ cross-section $M^+_{p_E}(t)$ dilutes as $|\psi|^2 \propto 1/A(t) = 1/(4\pi r^2)$ over the expanding Sphere surface $A(t) = 4\pi r^2$ (Theorem 28.5a, §38a.4): the $+ic$-monotonic growth of the surface carries the per-photon probability to a detector of area $A_\text{det}$ at distance $r$ with weight $A_\text{det}/(4\pi r^2)$.

For a source of known emission rate $R$ (photons per unit time — a standard candle), the expected detection rate at distance $r$ is the number flux
$$F = \frac{R}{4\pi r^2},$$
and inverting recovers the distance,
$$r = \sqrt{\frac{R}{4\pi F}}.$$
The distance unavailable from one photon (§38b.1) is recovered from the ensemble's inverse-square dilution: a fainter group of photons — fewer counts per unit detector area and time than an otherwise identical group — is the more distant source.

*Prior art (Ballentine, 1970; the luminosity-distance method).* Ballentine's statistical interpretation reads the quantum state as a statement about an ensemble: "the quantum state description may be taken to refer to an ensemble of similarly prepared systems" ([252], p. 47; [251]), with the Born probabilities fixing "the probability distributions of measurement results, not the individual measurement results themselves" ([251]). The inverse-square flux law $F = L/(4\pi r^2)$ and the standard-candle recovery of distance from a known luminosity are the classical photometric-distance method of observational astronomy ([253]).

*McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic reading.* The ensemble whose statistics make the Born rule manifest is, under the Principle, the family of photons riding one expanding McGucken Sphere, and the distribution Ballentine attaches to the ensemble is the SO(3)-Haar measure on the Sphere surface $4\pi r^2$ (Theorem 10.1; Theorem 28.5a). The inverse-square flux of the photometric method is that same Born density read over many photons: $F = R/(4\pi r^2)$ is the $1/A(t)$ dilution of $|\psi|^2$ across the $+ic$-expanding surface. The photometric distance and the quantum Born probability are one measure of the expanding Sphere, read at the ensemble scale.

## 38b.3 Theorem 28.12: Single-Photon Opacity and Ensemble Transparency of the Expanding Sphere

The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality. The following theorem makes the two readings of §§38b.1–38b.2 one result about one Sphere.

**Theorem 28.12 (Single-Photon Opacity and Ensemble Transparency, Grade 2; rests on Theorem 10.1 (measurement as 3-slice cross-section), Theorem 10.8 (M1′ measurement bound), Theorem 28.5a (Born dilution over the expanding Sphere), and Theorem 28.2 (photon-frame coincidence)).** *Let a point source at distance $r$ emit photons at number rate $R$, each as an SO(3)-isotropic amplitude on the McGucken Sphere of its emission event, with Born measure uniform over the fixed-$t$ cross-section $M^+(t)$ of radius $\rho = c(t - \tau_0)$ (Theorem 10.1). Then:*

*(i) **Single-photon opacity.** A single detection event fixes only the null relation $r = c(t_\text{det} - \tau_0)$ between the source distance $r$ and the unknown emission time $\tau_0$. Marginalized over $\tau_0$ under any prior, the Fisher information about $r$ from one detection is zero, and the source-position entropy is bounded below by $S_\text{loc} = k_B \ln(4\pi r^2)$ (Theorem 10.8). The detected photon's proper time and proper length along its null worldline are zero (Theorem 28.2), so its phase and its emission present reach the detector unchanged.*

*(ii) **Ensemble transparency.** For $N$ independent detections from a source of known rate $R$, the received number flux is $F = R/(4\pi r^2)$, the Born-number density of the ensemble over the Sphere surface $4\pi r^2$; inverting gives $r = \sqrt{R/(4\pi F)}$, with relative precision $\Delta r / r = 1/(2\sqrt{N})$ at Poisson-limited counting.*

*(iii) **One Sphere.** The per-photon Born weight $A_\text{det}/(4\pi r^2)$ and the ensemble flux $R/(4\pi r^2)$ are one quantity — the SO(3)-Haar probability measure of the expanding McGucken Sphere — read at one event and over many events.*

**Proof.** *(i)* The detection records $(t_\text{det}, \mathbf{x}_\text{det})$. The emission event lies on the past McGucken Sphere through $\mathbf{x}_\text{det}$, so $r$ and $\tau_0$ enter the single-click likelihood only through $r = c(t_\text{det} - \tau_0)$. Write the one-detection log-likelihood $\ell(r, \tau_0)$; along the null constraint it depends on the pair only through the combination $c(t_\text{det} - \tau_0) - r$, which the detection sets to zero. Marginalizing $\tau_0$ against any prior $\pi(\tau_0)$ leaves a likelihood independent of $r$ (every $r > 0$ is matched by the $\tau_0 = t_\text{det} - r/c$ that satisfies the constraint), so $\partial \ell / \partial r \equiv 0$ after marginalization and the Fisher information $\mathcal{I}(r) = \mathbb{E}[(\partial \ell/\partial r)^2] = 0$. The minimal localization entropy $S_\text{loc} = k_B \ln(4\pi r^2)$ is Theorem 10.8. The null worldline gives $ds^2 = 0$, hence $d\tau = 0$ and zero proper length (Theorem 28.2). *(ii)* By the SO(3)-Haar uniformity of the Born density on $M^+(t)$ (Theorem 10.1), the probability that an emitted photon crosses a detector of area $A_\text{det}$ at distance $r$ is $A_\text{det}/(4\pi r^2)$; for rate $R$ the expected count rate is $F A_\text{det}$ with $F = R/(4\pi r^2)$, and $r = \sqrt{R/(4\pi F)}$. For $N$ Poisson counts the relative uncertainty in $F$ is $1/\sqrt{N}$, and propagating through $r \propto F^{-1/2}$ gives $\Delta r / r = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\Delta F / F = 1/(2\sqrt{N})$. *(iii)* Both $A_\text{det}/(4\pi r^2)$ and $R/(4\pi r^2)$ are the Sphere's SO(3)-Haar measure on the surface $4\pi r^2$ (Theorem 10.1; Theorem 28.5a), evaluated per photon and summed over the ensemble. ∎

**Scope.** Theorem 28.12 assumes a known emission rate $R$ for the distance inversion of part (ii) — the standard-candle condition; without a known $R$ the ensemble flux fixes $R/r^2$ rather than $r$ alone. Part (i) is independent of any such condition: one detection fixes only the null relation whatever the source.

## 38b.4 Theorem 28.13: Quantized Collapse Conceals the Sphere's Nonlocality

The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality. The single-photon opacity of Theorem 28.12(i) is a consequence of how measurement reads the Sphere, which the next theorem states.

**Theorem 28.13 (Quantized Collapse Conceals the Sphere's Nonlocality, Grade 2; rests on Theorem 10.1 (measurement as 3-slice cross-section projection), Theorem 28.2 (photon-frame coincidence), and Theorems 28.4–28.5 (the two McGucken Laws of Nonlocality)).** *A single-photon detection is the 3-slice cross-section projection of Theorem 10.1 at the $+ic$-oriented detection event. This projection returns one definite event and conserves the photon's phase and emission present along its null worldline (Theorem 28.2). The SO(3)-distributed nonlocal probability of the expanding McGucken Sphere is carried by the photon but is not exhibited by the single outcome; it is exhibited operationally only in the ensemble (Theorem 28.12(ii)) and in the growth of the entanglement-origin Sphere at $c$ (Theorems 28.4–28.5). The nonlocality of the expanding Sphere is therefore concealed at the single-detection level by the quantized reading of measurement, and exhibited statistically.*

**Proof.** By Theorem 10.1 a measurement reads the spatial 3-slice cross-section of $\Psi$ at the detection event and projects onto the outcome eigenspace, returning one eigenvalue at one event. By Theorem 28.2 the photon's null worldline carries zero proper time, so the phase (unitary evolution) and the emission present are carried to the detector unchanged. A single projection returns one event and no distribution; the SO(3)-Haar Born measure over the Sphere surface is a property of the ensemble of detections (Theorem 28.12(ii)), not of the single click. The growth of the Sphere of potential entanglement at exactly $c$ (Theorem 28.5) is likewise a property of the Sphere's extent, not of any single detection. Hence the single detection is consistent with the full SO(3)-distributed Sphere probability while exhibiting none of it, and the nonlocality is exhibited only in the ensemble and in the Sphere's growth. ∎

**Relation to measurement defining physics.** Under the Principle, physics is defined by measurement, and the measured event is what exists (§14.9). Theorem 28.13 states the price of that definiteness for a single photon: the quantized measurement returns the event and conserves the photon's present, and the Sphere's nonlocal probability — carried in the amplitude — is read only when many events are taken together. The single photon and the ensemble are the same expanding Sphere; the quantized reading exhibits the event, the statistical reading exhibits the Sphere.

## 38b.5 The Readings of the Single Photon and the Ensemble

The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality. The table places the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic reading far-left against the prior art that each hold one face of the single-photon / ensemble duality.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| The single photon | Rides the Sphere; conserves its phase and present ($v_{x_4}=0$, zero proper time); one detection fixes only $r = c(t_\text{det}-\tau_0)$ | Spherical wave localizes to one point; read as a difficulty ("action at a distance") | One definite outcome; the state refers to the ensemble, not the single system | Carries no distance information |
| The ensemble | $1/r^2$ Born dilution over the expanding Sphere surface $4\pi r^2$ recovers $r$ | — (not addressed) | Born distribution manifest over many trials | Flux $F = L/(4\pi r^2)$ inverts to distance |
| The expanding sphere | Physical $dx_4/dt = ic$ wavefront; nonlocal, carries the SO(3)-Haar Born measure | Wavefunction that collapses on detection | No physical sphere; a statistical ensemble | Geometric flux surface $4\pi r^2$; no Born measure |
